*Ph.D. candidate in Quantitative & Computational Biosciences, Baylor College of Medicine · Houston, Texas*

## About

Daniel Palacios is an applied AI research scientist and PhD candidate in Quantitative & Computational Biosciences at Baylor College of Medicine, advised by Dr. Zhandong Liu in the Liu Lab at the Data Science Center, Texas Children's Hospital. His expertise is building AI systems that turn messy, real-world clinical data into answers people can act on — the full pipeline from raw records to validated results.

His day-to-day research falls into four areas:

- **Clinical outcome prediction:** designing AI agents and LLM systems that plan, code, debug, and interpret their own analyses to predict patient outcomes — postpartum depression risk (ClinPreAI), pediatric diabetes complications (CEDAR) — benchmarked against classical machine learning and deep learning.
- **Entity extraction:** pulling structure out of clinical text with LLMs — treatment-response phenotypes for rare disease research, and PHI scrubbing for clinical-note de-identification.
- **Foundation models:** training transformer-based models on electronic health records, including a generative pediatric EHR foundation model (TEDDY) trained on data from millions of children.
- **End-to-end data analysis:** raw data to ML-ready — data curation, large-scale pipelines, and biomedical statistics (risk factors, odds and hazard ratios, clustering), so analyses are rigorous before any model is trained.

The throughline is data: large-scale PySpark pipelines over standardized EHR data (OMOP CDM, Epic Clarity) on Palantir Foundry and AWS, feeding validated analyses and models.

Daniel is also an AI Developer and Research Design Intern at Peraton, where he builds LLM and multi-agent software and designs controlled experiments on how system design choices affect performance and reliability.

His path started in physics and mathematics at the University of Houston (B.S., magna cum laude, 2022), where his theoretical research on asymmetric superconductivity was published in Physical Review B. At NASA Ames Research Center, he built an agent-based model of radiation damage in microbial cells, validated against BioSentinel mission data. At NASA Johnson Space Center, he applied NLP to engineering failure reports, building a taxonomy for space-hardware failure analysis. That background shapes how he works: careful experimental design, rigorous evaluation, systems built to be trusted.

An NSF Graduate Research Fellow and NLM Fellow, Daniel has received Baylor's Dean's Award of Excellence and an Outstanding TA award. His work has been disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and 20+ conference presentations.
